content:
Mio looked away too quickly.

Until then, Touma had almost managed to believe the jokes were helping.

“They’ll look at me,” she said, “and start deciding.”

“Deciding what?”

“What category I go in. Whether I’m safe. Whether I’m supposed to be here.” She glanced at him. “Seeing me will be the easy part. Seeing anything except a problem—that might take some work.”

“We don’t have to make this public.”

“This is already not normal, Touma. Keeping it in a bedroom doesn’t make it normal.”

“I meant we could give you time. Take some of the pressure off.”

“You make it sound like you’re offering to remove my nervous system.”

“That wasn’t what I—”

“I know.”

Nico shifted beside the door.

“I’ll be outside,” he said, with the careful neutrality of someone trying not to admit how much he wanted to be outside.

He stepped into the hallway. Without him, the room seemed smaller.

Touma became aware of the quiet air conditioner, the edge of the futon beneath his legs, the chair pushed crookedly under the cheap desk. There were too few places to look without looking at Mio.

“Do you want to sit down?”

“Why? Am I making the room look haunted?”

“No.”

“Because I could stand in the corner and flicker. Really commit to the projector aesthetic.”

“I just thought you might want to sit.”

She studied the chair before pulling it out.

Touma tried not to watch too closely as she lowered herself onto it.

The chair squeaked.

That was all. A cheap chair protesting someone’s weight. It stayed beneath her. She stayed on it.

Relief loosened something in his chest so abruptly that he almost smiled.

“Don’t make that face,” Mio said.

“What face?”

“Like the furniture just approved my application.”

He looked down.

“Sorry.”

The room had made space for her. It was ridiculous how much that mattered.

When he looked up again, she was staring at her hands.

He had mistaken the expression for embarrassment before. Now he thought it might be what fear looked like when it had a face and was trying not to use it.

“Can you eat?” he asked.

Her eyes lifted.

He heard the question a moment too late.

“Sorry. That came out wrong.”

“No, it’s a reasonable question.” Her mouth moved without quite becoming a smile. “Apparently we’re doing reasonable questions now.”

“You don’t have to answer.”

“I’m not sure I can.”

He had wanted to offer something useful. Food. Water. A chair. Ordinary things people needed when they were frightened.

But he didn’t know what being in this body meant for her. Whether she got hungry. Whether sitting took effort. Whether anything hurt.

He wanted to take her hand.

His own hand moved against his knee before he stopped it. Wanting to reassure her did not mean he knew what touching her would do—or whether she wanted him to.

Mio noticed.

“You were going to ask something.”

From the hallway came the soft scuff of Nico’s shoe.

“I’m going to check downstairs,” Nico said.

“Wait,” Touma said automatically.

Nico stopped in the doorway. His eyes flicked toward Mio, then away.

Touma couldn’t think of a reason to keep him there that wasn’t selfish.

“Sorry. Go ahead.”

Nico nodded and left.

Mio was still watching Touma.

“I was going to ask if it hurt,” he said.

For a moment, the room did something wrong.

The edge of the desk seemed to shift without moving. Mio’s outline lost its certainty and returned before Touma could decide whether he had really seen it.

She held herself very still.

“Sometimes,” she said. “It feels like I’m trying too hard to hold a shape that makes sense.”

One of her fingers twitched against her knee.

He made himself keep his hands where they were.

“Then we should have some ground rules.”

“That sounds reassuringly bureaucratic.”

“No surprise touching.”

Her expression changed, just slightly.

“All right.”

“And tell me if something hurts.”

“Touma—”

“I don’t mean you have to explain it. Just tell me.”

“I don’t want to be a problem.”

He searched for an answer that wouldn’t make that sound easy.

“People are problems,” he said at last.

She stared at him.

“That was terrible.”

“I mean people need things. They hurt. They don’t always know what to do about it. That doesn’t mean they’re doing something wrong.”

“How inspirational.”

“If something’s wrong, tell me. I’ll listen.”

Her sarcasm faded without leaving anything comfortable in its place.

“You will?”

“Yes.”

“Even if it doesn’t make sense?”

“Yes.”

He left it there. Another promise would only give her more words to doubt.

She watched him for a long moment. He didn’t think she trusted him yet. But when her shoulders eased a little, he thought she might want to believe she could.

The support technician appeared in the doorway without knocking.

“Hey, I was told to check the—”

He stopped.

His gaze settled on Mio.

Touma saw the exact instant an ordinary errand became the wrong kind of miracle.

“Who is that?”

Mio went perfectly still.

Touma stood too fast, catching his heel against the futon.

“That’s not your business.”

The technician looked at him, then at Mio, then back again.

Something changed in his face. Not understanding. Something worse: the pleased, startled recognition of a person who had found a story worth telling.

Touma felt embarrassment and fear arrive together. The bedroom. The closed-off conversation. His own clumsy scramble to stand between them. Any detail could become evidence of whatever story the technician decided this was.

“Leave,” he said.

“I was just—”

“Please. Leave.”

The technician backed into the hallway.

Touma shut the door.

Behind him, Mio let out a breath.

“Well,” she said. “There goes my dramatic reveal.”

He kept his hand on the door for a moment.

That had been public.

Not an abstract risk anymore. Someone had looked at her while she sat frightened in a cheap chair, and now he could carry that look elsewhere. He could describe her. He could make people curious.

Touma turned.

Mio’s chin was raised, but her hands were pressed flat against her knees.

“Maybe he won’t say anything,” he said.

She looked at him.

“Right,” he said.

There were already too many eyes. It was too late to make this something that hadn’t happened.

“What do we do if people start asking?” she said.

“We lie.”

“Wonderful.”

“We can work out the details.”

“You are catastrophically bad at this.”

There was something almost affectionate beneath the disgust. It made him feel worse, and then, unfairly, better.

Mio looked toward the door.

“If I’m going to be seen,” she said, “I refuse to be seen as a mistake.”

Touma answered before he could make the words safer.

“You’re not a mistake.”

She looked back at him.

He felt exposed. There was no joke attached to what he had said, no practical task to hide inside. He could only let her hear it.

Mio gave a small, shaky laugh.

For one second, the room became bearable.

Then something scraped outside it.

Touma turned toward the door.

Not footsteps. Not the latch.

The sound came again, soft and deliberate, from the wall beside it: a fingertip dragging along the other side.

He stared at the plaster.

Nothing moved. Still, he had the distinct impression of pressure gathering behind it, something pressing close to the surface.

His limiter pulsed cold.

Not reassurance. A warning.

Mio’s chair creaked.

“Don’t let the system decide what I am,” she said.

Touma couldn’t look away from the wall.

The next scrape came deeper, as though something had heard her and leaned closer.
